claims.text: A circuit diagram uses standard symbols for every component it contains: a cell is a pair of parallel lines of unequal length, a battery of cells is a stack of such pairs, a resistor is a rectangle, a variable resistor is a rectangle with a diagonal arrow through it, a switch is a break in the wire with a line that can close it, and a lamp is a circle with a cross inside it.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Standard meter symbols: a circle with A inside is an ammeter, a circle with V inside is a voltmeter, and both are drawn in the wire where they belong, the ammeter in series and the voltmeter across the component.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A voltmeter is designed to have a very high resistance, and an ammeter is designed to have a very low resistance.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Standard symbols describe a circuit without drawing the components: a junction is a dot where three or more wires meet, and the same circuit can be described in a table (component, symbol name, value) or in words as an alternative to a drawn diagram.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: To interpret a circuit diagram, first identify the source and its e.m.f., then trace each complete path from the positive terminal back to the negative terminal, listing the components each path carries in order.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Components drawn one after another on the same unbranched path carry the same current: they are in series. Components drawn on separate branches between the same two junctions have the same potential difference across them: they are in parallel.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: An ammeter reads the current where it is connected, so an ammeter placed in series with a component measures the current in that component; a voltmeter reads the potential difference between the two points it is connected across.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The electromotive force (e.m.f.) of a source is the energy transferred from other forms to electrical energy per unit charge driven round a complete circuit: E = W/Q, with E in volts, W in joules and Q in coulombs.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: One volt is one joule per coulomb, so an e.m.f. of 6.0 V means 6.0 J of energy is given to each coulomb of charge that the source drives round the circuit.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The energy a source transfers is W = EIt, with W in joules, E the e.m.f. in volts, I the current in amperes and t the time in seconds, because Q = It.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Potential difference (p.d.) is the energy converted from electrical energy to other forms per unit charge that passes through a component; e.m.f. is the energy given to each unit of charge by a source. Both are measured in volts.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The e.m.f. of a source is the p.d. across its terminals when no current flows, because with no current there is no energy converted inside the source itself.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: E.m.f. is an energy gain per unit charge (other forms to electrical, inside the source); p.d. is an energy loss per unit charge (electrical to other forms, in the external components). The test: is the energy going into the circuit or out of it?

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The internal resistance of a source is the resistance inside the source itself; the current flowing through it produces a p.d. Ir across it, which makes the terminal p.d. less than the e.m.f. whenever a current flows.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Terminal p.d. V = E − Ir, with V the terminal p.d. in volts, E the e.m.f. in volts, I the current in amperes and r the internal resistance in ohms. The quantity Ir is the p.d. across the internal resistance, sometimes called the lost volts.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: When the current increases, the terminal p.d. falls, because the p.d. Ir across the internal resistance grows with the current; when no current flows the terminal p.d. equals the e.m.f.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A source with internal resistance r connected to an external resistance R drives a current I = E/(R + r), because the e.m.f. drives the current round the whole circuit, internal and external.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Kirchhoff's first law: the total current entering a junction equals the total current leaving the junction. It is a consequence of conservation of charge, because charge neither accumulates at nor vanishes from a junction.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Kirchhoff's first law applies at a junction, a point where three or more conductors meet; it is stated about currents at that point, not about the current round a loop.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Kirchhoff's second law: the sum of the e.m.f.s round a closed loop equals the sum of the potential differences round that loop. It is a consequence of conservation of energy, because a unit of charge returning to its starting point has neither gained nor lost energy.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Kirchhoff's second law applies round a closed loop, not at a junction: the first law is about currents at a junction, the second about energies round a loop. The test: a junction or a loop?

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: In a series circuit the current is the same everywhere, so the e.m.f. equals the sum of the p.d.s across the components; in a single-loop circuit this is Kirchhoff's second law written out.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: For resistors in series, each carries the same current I (first law: no junction between them) and the p.d.s add to the supply p.d. (second law), so V = V1 + V2 + V3 = IR1 + IR2 + IR3 and the combined resistance is R = R1 + R2 + R3.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The derivation of the series formula uses both laws: Kirchhoff's first law gives the same current through every resistor, and Kirchhoff's second law gives the p.d.s adding to the supply p.d. Only because the current is the same can the I be factored out.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The combined resistance of resistors in series is greater than the largest single resistance, because the same current must push through every resistor one after another.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: For resistors R1, R2, R3 in series, the combined resistance is R = R1 + R2 + R3, and each resistor takes a share of the supply p.d. in proportion to its resistance: V1 = IR1.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Adding a resistor in series always increases the combined resistance; for two equal resistors R in series the combined resistance is 2R.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: For resistors in parallel, each branch has the same p.d. V across it (second law, comparing the loop through each branch) and the currents add (first law), so I = I1 + I2 + I3 = V/R1 + V/R2 + V/R3, giving 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The derivation of the parallel formula uses the laws the other way round from the series derivation: the same p.d. across each branch from the second law, the currents adding at the junction from the first law.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: For resistors in parallel, 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3, and the combined resistance R is smaller than the smallest single resistance, because the current has more than one path.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Adding a branch in parallel always lowers the combined resistance, because the new branch gives the current another route; two equal resistors R in parallel have a combined resistance of R/2.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: In the parallel formula the reciprocals add and the final step takes the reciprocal again: for 4.0 Ω and 12 Ω in parallel, 1/R = 1/4.0 + 1/12 = 0.333..., so R = 3.0 Ω.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: To solve a circuit with Kirchhoff's laws: mark the current in each branch, apply the first law at each junction to relate the currents, then apply the second law round each closed loop to relate the e.m.f.s to the p.d.s.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A circuit with one e.m.f. and resistors in series and parallel is solved by combining the resistances stepwise into one total resistance, finding the supply current from I = E/Rtotal, then splitting the p.d. and current back down through the combinations.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The current in a branch between the same two junctions divides in inverse proportion to the branch resistances: the branch with the smaller resistance carries the larger current.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A potential divider is two or more resistors in series across a supply; the supply p.d. is shared between them in the ratio of their resistances, and the p.d. across one resistor is a fraction of the supply p.d.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: For two resistors R1 and R2 in series across a supply of p.d. V, the p.d. across R1 is V1 = R1/(R1 + R2) × V, because the same current flows through both and V1 = IR1.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The supply p.d. in a divider is shared between all the resistors in series, so no single resistor takes the whole supply p.d.; the sum of the p.d.s equals the supply p.d.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A potentiometer is a uniform resistance wire or track of length L across which a known p.d. is applied; the p.d. between one end and a sliding contact at length x is x/L × V, because the p.d. is shared in proportion to length as resistance is uniform.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A potentiometer compares two p.d.s without drawing current from them: the sliding contact is moved until the p.d. it taps equals the unknown p.d., and the balance lengths on the wire are in the ratio of the two p.d.s being compared, so V1/V2 = x1/x2.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A potentiometer is used in preference to a voltmeter to compare p.d.s because at balance no current is drawn from the source being measured, so its internal resistance does not reduce the reading.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A galvanometer is a sensitive meter that detects current in either direction and reads zero at the centre of its scale; in a null method it is connected between the two points whose p.d.s are being compared, and the sliding contact is adjusted until it reads zero.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: At the balance point of a null method the galvanometer reads zero: no current flows through it, so the two p.d.s it sits between are equal. The balance point is found, not a vague region.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A null method compares p.d.s without drawing current at balance, which is why the comparison does not disturb the very circuit it measures.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A thermistor is a resistor whose resistance falls as its temperature rises; a light-dependent resistor (LDR) is a resistor whose resistance falls as the light intensity on it rises.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: In a potential divider with a thermistor, a rise in temperature lowers the thermistor's resistance, so the p.d. across the fixed resistor rises and the p.d. across the thermistor falls; the output is taken across one of the two.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: In a potential divider with an LDR, an increase in light intensity lowers the LDR's resistance, so the p.d. across the fixed resistor rises; a divider can switch an output on or off as light or temperature crosses a threshold.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Whether a divider's output p.d. rises or falls when the sensor's resistance falls depends on which component the output is taken across: taken across the fixed resistor it rises, taken across the sensor it falls.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 10 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).
